title: The tools
sub: Counters, heap snapshots, traces and dumps
cards/0/body:
• dotnet-counters — what is happening right now: heap size, collections, pauses, allocation rate;
  • dotnet-gcdump — which types occupy the heap and who holds them;
  • dotnet-trace — what happened over a span of time: every collection, who allocates;
  • dotnet-dump — the full memory of the process: field values, threads, everything at once;
  • PerfView — an analyzer for Windows: opens traces and snapshots, compares them.

The first four are cross-platform .NET utilities. They install as global tools: dotnet tool install --global dotnet-counters. With the .NET 10 SDK you can also run them without installing: dnx dotnet-counters.
cards/0/code:
dotnet tool install --global dotnet-counters
dotnet-counters ps        # which .NET processes are visible
cards/0/deep: All four talk to the runtime through the diagnostic port: a named pipe on Windows, a Unix socket in the temp folder on Linux and macOS. Hence the common problems: the tool must run as the same user as the process (or as root), with the same TMPDIR, and for a container you either install the tool inside or expose the socket and pass --diagnostic-port. Back in .NET Framework none of this existed: there were Windows performance counters, ETW and WinDbg with SOS.
cards/1/body:
dotnet-counters monitor attaches to a process and refreshes a table every second. collect writes the same to CSV or JSON.

Since .NET 9 the runtime publishes the System.Runtime meter with new names. For memory, watch:

  • dotnet.gc.last_collection.heap.size — the heap by generation after the last collection;
  • dotnet.gc.last_collection.heap.fragmentation.size — the gaps;
  • dotnet.gc.last_collection.memory.committed_size — the GC commit;
  • dotnet.gc.heap.total_allocated — total allocated; its growth gives the allocation rate;
  • dotnet.gc.collections and dotnet.gc.pause.time — collections and pauses;
  • dotnet.process.memory.working_set.
cards/1/deep: If the app runs on .NET 8 or older, there is no System.Runtime meter, and the tool shows the old EventCounters: gc-heap-size, gen-0-size, gen-2-size, loh-size, poh-size, alloc-rate, time-in-gc, gc-fragmentation, gc-committed (since .NET 6), working-set. Without --counters it shows all of System.Runtime by default. The same metrics can be exported to OpenTelemetry and viewed on a dashboard — counters is for a quick look without any setup.
cards/2/q: Match the question with the System.Runtime counter in .NET 9+
cards/2/pairs/0/0: How many bytes per second the code allocates
cards/2/pairs/2/0: How long threads stood still in collections
cards/2/pairs/3/0: Whether the heap has many gaps
cards/2/pairs/4/0: How much of the process is in RAM now
cards/3/q: Save the counters of process 1902 to a table so you can plot them later
cards/3/explain: monitor only draws a table in the terminal; collect writes to a file. The formats of collect are csv and json; nettrace and speedscope are dotnet-trace formats.
cards/4/title: dotnet-gcdump: the heap graph without values
cards/4/body:
dotnet-gcdump collect -p 1902 asks the runtime to perform a full generation 2 collection and, during it, to emit events about every object and the references between them. The tool builds a graph from them and writes a .gcdump file.

The file holds types, sizes, references and roots. No field values: no strings, no numbers. So the file is small, safe to hand over, and good for the question "what takes up memory and who holds it".

The price: a full blocking collection, a long pause on a large heap. You open a .gcdump in Visual Studio or PerfView; on Linux you can get a type table: dotnet-gcdump report file.gcdump.
cards/4/deep: The events go through a buffer inside the process itself, which can grow up to 256 MB — keep that in mind in a container with a tight limit. On a very large heap events can be dropped and the snapshot comes out incomplete; take a full dump then. By default collect waits 30 seconds (-t changes the timeout). Visual Studio can open two .gcdump files and compare them.
cards/5/q: A cache holds thousands of strings. You need to see which URLs exactly are in them. What do you capture?
cards/5/options/3: A trace with the gc-collect profile
cards/5/explain: Object contents exist only in a full memory dump: dumpheap finds the strings, dumpobj shows their text. A .gcdump holds only types, sizes and references, and counters and gc-collect know nothing about individual objects.
cards/5/wrong/1: A heap snapshot shows how many strings there are and who holds them, but not their text: a .gcdump has no field values.
cards/6/title: dotnet-dump: all of memory, plus SOS
cards/6/body:
dotnet-dump collect -p 1902 writes a dump. --type sets the kind: Full (the default, all memory including module images), Heap (all memory except mapped images), Mini and Triage (stacks and modules, no heap). Memory analysis needs Full or Heap. The file is as big as the process’s memory and contains everything: passwords, tokens, customer data.

dotnet-dump analyze file opens a console with SOS commands:

  • dumpheap -stat — types by total size, the largest at the bottom;
  • dumpheap -mt <MT> — addresses of objects of one type;
  • dumpobj <address> — an object’s fields;
  • gcroot <address> — the path from a root to the object;
  • eeheap -gc, finalizequeue, gchandles — heap segments, the finalization queue, handles.
cards/6/deep: You can also get a dump at the moment of a crash, without the tool: the environment variables DOTNET_DbgEnableMiniDump=1 and DOTNET_DbgMiniDumpType (1 — Mini, 2 — Heap, 3 — Triage, 4 — Full). In a container collect needs the ptrace capability, and taking a full dump can temporarily raise memory use — with a hard limit the container risks being killed. Back in .NET Framework the same was done with WinDbg and the SOS extension; dotnet-dump has the same commands, without a native debugger.
cards/7/q: Put the steps of a dump analysis in order
cards/7/explain: First take the dump and open it. Then statistics by type — find the suspicious type and its MT. By MT, list the instances and take an address from it. And for that address, the path to a root.
cards/8/body:
A heap snapshot shows what survived. If the problem is that the code allocates a lot and the GC runs nonstop, you need a trace.

dotnet-trace collect -p 1902 --profile gc-verbose records the events of every collection (reason, generation, pause) and a sample of allocations: roughly every 100 KB of allocated memory, an AllocationTick event with the object type and the call stack. Aggregating them shows which methods allocate the most. The gc-collect profile records only collections, with minimal overhead.

The result is a .nettrace file. You open it in PerfView or Visual Studio.
cards/8/deep: Profiles have changed between tool versions: in recent dotnet-trace, running without --profile enables dotnet-common and dotnet-sampled-thread-time, and collect no longer has the old cpu-sampling profile. The profiles of your version: dotnet-trace list-profiles. The speedscope format is fine for CPU stacks, but GC events need nettrace. AllocationTick is a sample, not every allocation: rare small allocations may not make it in.
cards/9/q: Counters show 2 GB of allocations per second and 40 gen0 collections per second, but the heap does not grow. What do you capture to find the culprit?
cards/9/options/0: A dotnet-trace trace with the gc-verbose profile
cards/9/options/1: Two dotnet-gcdump snapshots, then compare them
cards/9/options/2: A dotnet-dump dump of type Mini
cards/9/explain: The heap does not grow, so the objects die quickly and snapshots barely contain them. The answer to "who allocates" comes from allocation stacks in a trace. A Mini dump has no heap, and counters know nothing about stacks.
cards/10/body:
PerfView is Microsoft’s free analyzer for Windows. It collects traces through ETW — with kernel events and every process on the machine — and opens .nettrace and .gcdump files captured on Linux.

For memory it has three key things:

  • GCStats — a table of every collection in a trace: generation, reason, pause, heap size before and after;
  • a heap snapshot (Memory → Take Heap Snapshot) and a view of the paths to roots;
  • Diff — comparing two snapshots or two traces against a baseline.
cards/10/deep: On a large heap PerfView by default builds the snapshot from a sample of objects and scales the numbers, so its sizes are approximate — a full dump gives exact figures. Traces and snapshots captured on Linux are analyzed by moving the file to a Windows machine. Back in the .NET Framework era PerfView and WinDbg were the main tools; today PerfView is still the most detailed viewer of GC events.
